resources.string: QEMU\'s built-in VNC server. This is the only way a Windows guest can be seen — it has no X server of its own. Linux guests use the in-guest Xvnc on 5900 instead.

When off, VNC is loopback-only and reachable from the in-app viewer. When on, it listens on 0.0.0.0 — the same port becomes reachable from any device on the same Wi-Fi, so connect from a desktop VNC client using this phone\'s IP address.

UEFI is the default. Switch to BIOS only if the disk was installed without an EFI System Partition — otherwise the guest drops to a UEFI Shell.
The in-app X11 preview connects to this same port. Windows guests have no X server of their own, so this is the only way to see the screen.
VNC is off, so the guest screen is not reachable anywhere — the preview will stay black. Turn it on to watch the boot.
The Windows screen renders through the in-app X11 preview — the only way to see a graphical guest.
No console output yet. A Windows guest writes nothing here while the installer or the desktop has the display; firmware and bootloader messages appear until it switches to graphics.
Nothing here by design — SeaBIOS writes to the VGA screen, not the serial port. Open the X11 preview to watch the boot.

Packs the container\'s whole current filesystem into one tar. Filesystem contents only — no image layers or config, so restoring it elsewhere means re-creating ports, volumes and environment. Tap Restore image on the archive in the list below to import it.

Exports every container currently in the VM — no name needed. Produces nothing if there are none yet.

Saves the image with all of its layers and metadata. After restoring it matches the original and the same container runs again — the one to use. Usually several times larger than an export. Fill in repository:tag, e.g. docker.io/library/nginx:latest — or tap an image in the list above and it fills in for you.
Pulls Docker Hub images through this mirror; only applies to docker.io references. With a mirror set, Save image pulls through it first, then archives.

Images are there, but there are no containers. Images are only the material: exporting a container and backing all containers up act on containers, so there is nothing in the list to tap. Start one in the VM (for example nginx) and read the list again.

Browse Downloads for a qcow2/img/raw/iso image. Tap a file to select it; the VM then boots from it via UEFI.
Both emulators target the same QEMU release. The x86_64 one runs Windows guests and needs a much larger memory allocation.
Press Start on the home screen; the first boot takes a while. Once the VM is up, the terminal button opens a root shell inside it.
# SSH from your phone into the VM\nssh root@localhost -p 9922
Containers are created inside the VM with whichever engine it has. This starts an Nginx web server that keeps running in the background.
A port published with -p is reachable from the phone at localhost. In the example above, 8080 is the port to open on the phone and 80 is the port inside the container.
# from a browser on the phone\nhttp://localhost:8080
Backups are plain tar archives written to the shared folder. They can also be created and restored from the container backup screen.
Things that trip people up, and what to try.
A backup has no containers in it - a stopped container still has to be exported before it is archived, so make sure it is running first. docker ps shows what the VM currently holds.
The scan finds no containers - they may live in a different engine, or have been removed. Run docker ps or podman ps in the terminal to see what the VM actually holds.
An image will not pull - usually the VM has no network route, or the registry is blocked. Check that the VM can reach the network, and use a mirror source if one is available.
Move or share a backup - the archives are ordinary tar files in the shared folder, so they can be copied or synced like any other file. Restore reads from that same folder.

The Windows guest cannot reach the internet. DHCP hands out an IP (10.0.2.x) from QEMU\'s built-in NAT, but its nameserver is a proxy that forwards through the phone, which is unreliable. Set the Windows adapter\'s DNS directly to 223.5.5.5 and 8.8.8.8 in the network adapter settings, and web pages load again. Ping still fails either way - the NAT does not forward ICMP.
